content: Routine data collection should focus on widely available information and be limited to essential figures that summarize program performance and describe basic aspects of data quality. A streamlined approach, emphasizing a few key indicators with appropriate disaggregation, can be highly effective. Ideally, platforms used to generate these data displays should allow managers to interact with the data, enabling further exploration of unexpected results. This includes assessing whether poor data quality is a factor or if the results genuinely reflect program performance. Such tools can serve as the foundation for routine cascade data review meetings or, at the very least, provide standardized analytic outputs for decision-making. For example, a subset of 11 program cascade indicators, derived from 15 national core indicators, is recommended for routine analysis. These indicators are supported by data dashboards, explanations for their use and interpretation, and training exercises to help program managers understand the dashboard figures. The World Health Organization (WHO) has provided guidance for HIV program managers on the analysis and use of health facility data, including a consolidated framework for strategic information. The HIV cascade dashboard offers a cross-sectional view of the percentages of people living with HIV who are diagnosed, linked to treatment, and have achieved viral suppression. This analysis is conducted at both national and subnational levels, as well as for priority populations. In 2018, WHO and its partners published the Cascade Data Use Manual, which provides examples of cascade analysis using various data types for different program management purposes. These include cascades specific to HIV treatment, prevention of mother-to-child transmission (PMTCT), and patient groups with co-morbidities such as HIV and tuberculosis (TB), hepatitis B, or hepatitis C. The cascade approach can also be applied to prevention efforts, tracking both HIV-positive and HIV-negative members of high-risk groups, including key populations. The manual outlines key steps for conducting and using cascade data analyses, such as assessing data quality, identifying gaps, and applying strategies to address common deficiencies. While aggregate data-based cascade analyses have limitations, particularly in countries with lower service coverage, they can still provide valuable insights into service access gaps. Countries with individual-level health information systems (HIS) and unique identification standards (UIS) can perform more robust cascade analyses, as these systems allow for deduplication and comprehensive tracking. However, in the absence of electronic tools and UIS, countries must rely on more complex paper-based systems designed for cohort analysis. Routine data reviews can be expanded to inform specific program improvements. QI involves measuring performance using standardized indicators, identifying quality challenges, exploring root causes, designing context-specific solutions, and assessing their impact through iterative testing. Many HIV programs use QI methods tailored to local capacity and resources, often employing the Plan-Do-Study-Act (PDSA) cycle. Regardless of the model used, HIV programs should institutionalize a culture of improvement across all levels, integrating QI into routine cascade data review activities. The emergence of HIV drug resistance (HIVDR) to antiretroviral therapy (ART), particularly to non-nucleoside reverse transcriptase inhibitors (NNRTIs) and nucleoside reverse transcriptase inhibitors (NRTIs), poses a global challenge. Resistance levels have exceeded 10% among adults initiating first-line ART in many countries. The introduction of dolutegravir (DTG), an integrase inhibitor, has mitigated NNRTI resistance trends. However, ongoing surveillance and efforts to prevent the emergence and transmission of HIVDR remain critical. WHO recommends integrating HIVDR prevention, monitoring, and response into national HIV programs and routine cascade data reviews. Establishing systems for routine data reviews involves several steps. First, convene the appropriate group of individuals, including programmatic, technical, and data experts, to participate in the review process. Define their roles and responsibilities for analysis, interpretation, documentation, and follow-up. Second, develop a plan for standardized core analyses, specifying priority indicators, disaggregations, and analytic outputs. Third, translate the findings into actionable steps for managers, ensuring accountability and coordination across management levels. Electronic health information systems (HIS) play a crucial role in supporting routine data reviews. These systems should collect, organize, analyze, and report data in a way that facilitates programmatic decision-making. WHO has developed supplemental materials to help countries incorporate standardized HIV metadata into digital systems. Countries should adopt interoperable data platforms across all geographic areas and health facility levels to optimize program management. Data visualization tools, such as dashboards, can enhance the usability of routine data by providing dynamic analytics and linking national and regional gap analyses to facility-level planning. Strategic information (SI) systems are essential for effective decision-making. Prioritizing program indicators is a key step in strengthening SI systems, as a smaller number of indicators improves data quality and usability. WHO recommends a top tier of 15 national core indicators for all countries, covering critical aspects of the HIV cascade. These indicators form the basis for routine data reviews to improve programs at national, district, and facility levels. Countries with robust HIS capacity may also consider an expanded set of 40 national priority indicators, which include the core 15. Countries are encouraged to customize their national core and priority indicators based on their specific context, focusing on those most relevant to their programmatic needs. Additional indicators may be selected for in-depth assessments of specific program areas or to address new initiatives, short-term efforts, or programmatic transitions. In summary, routine data reviews, supported by robust HIS and standardized indicators, are critical for monitoring and improving HIV programs. By prioritizing key indicators, ensuring data quality, and fostering a culture of continuous improvement, countries can enhance program performance and achieve better health outcomes.
